name: Uvinul A Plus

lead: Uvinul A Plus is a photostable UVA filter found in EU sunscreens, chosen by people who want strong UVA protection against skin aging and pigmentation. Absorbing UVA means less photoaging and fewer dark spots over time.

It is also known as diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB, Parsol DHHB), absorbs UVA with a peak near 354 nm, and is used in the EU at up to 10 percent. Published material covers chemistry and a 2020 human metabolism study rather than appearance outcomes.

paras: People look for DHHB on ingredient lists of European sunscreens and daily facial products, usually combined with other filters, and apply it as an everyday morning step. It is not a US sunscreen active.
The EU safety committee flagged a manufacturing impurity (di-n-hexyl phthalate) and recommended limits. Human metabolism was studied after oral and dermal doses in 2020.

angle.text: Uvinul A Plus is a photostable UVA filter found in EU sunscreens, sought by users who want strong UVA protection against skin aging and pigmentation. Absorbing UVA means less photoaging and fewer dark spots over time.

lead: Uvinul A Plus is BASF's trade name for diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB, also sold as Parsol DHHB), an organic UVA-absorbing sunscreen filter. It is used in sunscreens and other cosmetics in the European Union at up to 10 percent, and is described as photostable.[1][2]

It helps appearance through photoaging protection. UVA penetrates deeper into skin than UVB and is associated with damage that is not visible as redness, and Wikipedia's sunscreen article says sunlight is a major driver of premature aging and that daily broad-spectrum sunscreen use has been associated with smoother, more resilient skin.[3] A UVA filter such as DHHB is one way formulators build the UVA side of broad-spectrum protection into a sunscreen.[3]

Available research on the filter itself is chemical and toxicokinetic: a 2017 photophysics study, a 2020 human metabolism study, a 2019 urinary biomonitoring method and a 2021 water-degradation study.[1][2][4][5] No trials of appearance outcomes for this filter alone were found.

paras: DHHB is mainly used in sunscreens, and also appears in other cosmetic products, with a maximum concentration of 10 percent under the EU directive.[1][4] Wikipedia's sunscreen article notes that the EU approves more UV filters than the US because the US treats sunscreen as an over-the-counter drug while the EU treats it as a cosmetic.[3]

A 2017 photophysical study examined DHHB through transient absorption, emission, phosphorescence and electron paramagnetic resonance spectra, describing it as a photostable UVA absorber.[2] Wikipedia lists a maximum absorbance of 354 nm. Most organic UV filters do not break down significantly in sunlight, according to the sunscreen article.[3]

Wikipedia states that the EU approved DHHB for sunscreens in 2005 at up to 10 percent, and that it is also approved in several countries including Japan and Mexico but is not a US sunscreen active. The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety flagged possible contamination with di-n-hexyl phthalate from manufacturing and recommended limits on the impurity.

A 2020 study gave volunteers a single oral or dermal dose and followed metabolism and urinary excretion over 72 hours; three major urinary metabolites accounted for 52% of the oral dose.[1] A 2019 method for measuring metabolites in urine found them in about 36% of 58 samples from the general German population.[4] A 2021 study found DHHB degrades quickly under drinking-water disinfection conditions,[5] and a 2025 study characterized a human metabolite and its toxicity in a bioluminescence assay.[6]
A 2020 human study examined metabolism and urinary excretion after single oral and dermal exposure.[1] No studies of skin-appearance or photoprotection outcomes for this filter alone were found.

timeline.event: EU approves DHHB as a sunscreen filter at up to 10 percent.
